title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson about incident discipline, what is the central focus?
options: A history of incident management software
A review of unrelated debugging tools
Diagnosing a broken agent methodically under client pressure, by establishing ground truth, diagnosing before patching, and verifying a fix
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the discipline that kills the rush to patch and keeps a live failure from becoming a crisis.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Under pressure, change something quickly and claim it is fixed
A fix is a conclusion, not a first action: diagnose first, then patch, then verify
A confident wrong explanation sounds better than admitting you do not know
Assume the software is the cause so you debug the code first
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that skipping diagnosis means guessing, and a patch on top of a wrong diagnosis entangles the failure.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Status reflects a hopeful prediction of when the system will recover
A confident recovery time builds more trust than a humble honest one
Write the failure mode down only after the incident when details are calm
Report what you know, label what you do not, and commit to a cadence of honest updates rather than one invented timeline
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a confident wrong timeline destroys more trust than a humble correct one, so you commit to a stream of honest updates.

questions.question: Per the lesson about change management as a deliverable, what is the central focus?
options: Treating change to a live delivery as its own deliverable with scope, risk, test, rollback, and record, not a drive-by edit
A history of version control
A review of unrelated config tools
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a live delivery drifts one small unrecorded edit at a time unless change is treated as a bounded, visible deliverable.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A drive-by edit feels small because nothing breaks visibly, so it needs no record
Bundling extra unrequested edits into an approved change is efficient and harmless
Scope the change like a mini-engagement: what changes, what does not, who approves, and how to roll back
Trust your own judgment over a test because you built the original
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that each meaningful change answers the same questions as the original build in miniature, turning a drive-by edit into a visible deliverable.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The rollback plan is improvised after the change lands
The rollback is the most important artifact and must be written before the change, specific to the exact prior state
A change to a system that runs itself needs no gates because nobody is watching anyway
Tell the client about a high-risk change after it lands since the output looks the same
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a change that cannot be rolled back cleanly is a change you cannot afford to be wrong about, so the revert is written before the change.

questions.question: Per the lesson about handover that makes the client self-sufficient, what is the central focus?
options: Transferring ownership so the client can run, change, and recover the system, with operating docs, runbooks, a dry run, and a taper
A history of documentation tools
A review of unrelated wiki software
A summary of IT policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the deliverable is the agent plus the knowledge of how to operate it, transferred so your presence becomes optional.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: File handover, producing the artifacts, is the whole job
The operating doc is reference and the runbook is procedure, and the two answer different questions
Write the runbook for the engineer who built the thing
A document you wrote is proven once it is written
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the operating doc answers how the system is configured while the runbook tells a stranger what to do when something breaks.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The handover is real when you narrate the demo to the client
Secrets belong in the operating doc so the operator knows the values
The dry run has an unbriefed operator recover a deliberately failed run using only the runbook while you stay silent
Leave on a single day so the client owns it immediately
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the handover passes when an unbriefed stranger can run the recovery procedure to a successful end while you say nothing.

questions.question: Per the lesson about managing a small portfolio of clients, what is the central focus?
options: Keeping several engagements alive and honest by defending scope, holding expectations, and allocating time across the whole set
A history of client management software
A review of unrelated calendar tools
A summary of finance policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a portfolio is several commitments sharing one brain, and the craft is naming, measuring, and controlling the three enemies.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Scope creep in one engagement is harmless because it is extra work
One client per profile makes the scope boundary an architectural fact rather than a mental reminder
Promising an hour response time to every client is the honest move
Run committed hours at one hundred percent of capacity to maximize output
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a profile isolates each client's config, memory, skills, and jobs, so scope separation is enforced by the platform.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Spread each client's work thinly across the week to stay responsive
Let the loudest client extract whatever time they need that week
The weekly portfolio review forces the whole set into view so a quiet client does not quietly starve
Deliver every routine report by hand to keep quality high
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the engagement in front of you always demands attention, so a fixed weekly review catches the client you are not looking at.

questions.question: Per the lesson about vendor-agnostic translation, what is the central focus?
options: Separating the transferable discipline from the tool-specific mechanics so the playbook works on whatever agent a client runs
A history of agent vendors
A review of unrelated integration tools
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that your expertise is the playbook, not the tool, and the discipline transfers while the mechanics do not.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Copy the Hermes artifact into the new tool's format and the discipline follows
Force the new tool to be Hermes by building fake structures for concepts it never had
Map each intent to the primitive that genuinely carries it, then verify the behavior held in the new tool
Memorize the exact config syntax of every agent tool because it is the valuable layer
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the three-layer model: intent, mapping, and implementation, and to map each intent to a real primitive and verify it holds.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A translation worked when the files are in place in the new format
An honest capability gap is a deliverable with a price and a sign-off, not something to paper over
If a tool has no primitive for an intent, improvise a fragile approximation and call it done
A behavioral instruction is a structural guardrail as long as it is written well
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that when a tool cannot hold an intent, you name the gap with its price and options rather than trusting it will be fine.
